claim.why_it_matters: The '(combining)' qualifier of each combining-marks row is cut off its row label and left as a stray paragraph after the table, so the table shows two indistinguishable rows per script (e.g. two 'Arabic:' rows) and the combining-mark ranges read as ordinary letters. The distinction matters: B.3.1's NOTE limits combining marks to level 2 and extended-letter rules treat combining marks differently from letters. The table is also broken into several fragments with mixed table/paragraph rendering (Greek, Bengali onward as paragraphs).

verdict.reasoning: Checked the 300-dpi render of PDF page 790 (printed p.766, Annex repertoire table). In the PDF each combining row label wraps onto a second line ('Hebrew' / '(combining):', 'Arabic:' / '(Combining', etc.). The markdown keeps every word and every code-point range; the wrapped second line of each label lands as a paragraph immediately after the two-row table it belongs to, directly below the combining row. All ranges match the PDF exactly, and the PDF's own typos ('Hebrew' without a colon, '(Combining' with no closing parenthesis) are reproduced faithfully. Nothing is missing or misplaced to another entry: the qualifier sits on the adjacent line after its row, which is line-wrap reflow of a two-line table label. The table/paragraph mix (Greek, Bengali onward) is rendering format only. Under the refutation criteria (text present on an adjacent line; formatting/line-wrap only; meaning recoverable) this is not a content discrepancy.
